questions.q: A 32-year-old presents with sudden worsening of a single hypopigmented hypoaesthetic plaque on the forearm, with new satellite lesions and severe tenderness of the ulnar nerve. He is on treatment for borderline tuberculoid leprosy. Which type of lepra reaction is this?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction occurs in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL) due to a sudden increase in cell-mediated immunity. Features include worsening of existing lesions, new lesions, and acute neuritis. Treatment is prednisolone.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters involving the oral mucosa and skin. Nikolsky sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposits in the epidermis. Which antigen is primarily targeted by the pathogenic antibodies in the mucosal-dominant type?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris mucosal-dominant type is caused by antibodies against desmoglein 3. Mucocutaneous PV involves antibodies against both desmoglein 1 and 3. Pemphigus foliaceus targets desmoglein 1 only, sparing mucosae.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with circular scaly patches on the scalp with broken hair stubs. Wood's lamp examination reveals bright green fluorescence. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.exp: Microsporum species (M. canis, M. audouinii) cause ectothrix tinea capitis and produce bright green fluorescence under Wood's lamp. Trichophyton species (T. tonsurans, T. violaceum) cause endothrix infection and do not fluoresce.

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with a generalized maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, non-tender generalised lymphadenopathy, and mucous patches in the mouth. VDRL titre is 1:64. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose is the treatment of choice for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis. Doxycycline for 14 days is the alternative in penicillin allergy. The clinical picture describes secondary syphilis.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with a malar rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, and renal involvement. ANA is positive (1:640). Which antibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and also correlates with disease activity?
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific for SLE (>95% specificity) and their titres correlate with disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis. Anti-Ro is associated with subacute cutaneous LE and neonatal LE. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 72-year-old man presents with tense blisters on an urticarial base predominantly on flexural areas of the trunk and thighs. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the primary autoantigen?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is caused by IgG autoantibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen, NC16A domain) and BP230 at hemidesmosomes. The subepidermal blister results in tense blisters. Laminin 332 is targeted in mucous membrane pemphigoid and epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA).

questions.q: A patient presents with hypopigmented, finely scaling macules on the upper trunk. Wood's lamp examination reveals a specific fluorescence. Regarding pityriasis versicolor, which Wood's lamp finding is correct?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia furfur) shows golden-yellow or copper-orange fluorescence under Wood's lamp due to pityriacitrin. Erythrasma (Corynebacterium minutissimum) shows coral-red. Tinea capitis (Microsporum) shows bright green. Vitiligo shows bright white.

questions.q: A 38-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T6 dermatome following a prodrome of pain. A Tzanck smear from the blister base shows multinucleated giant cells. This finding is diagnostic of:
opts: Herpes simplex or varicella-zoster virus infection
questions.exp: Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells) is positive in all herpetic infections — HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV. It cannot differentiate between them. Molluscum contagiosum shows Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies on Tzanck smear.

questions.q: A 25-year-old develops symmetric target lesions (three concentric zones) on the palms, dorsa of hands, and forearms, 10 days after a labial herpes simplex episode. There is no mucosal involvement and no systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema multiforme minor features classic three-zone target lesions on acral sites, often triggered by HSV. EM major involves mucosal membranes. SJS is drug-triggered, involves >2 mucosal sites, and >10% BSA detachment. Fixed drug eruption recurs at the same site.

questions.q: A patient with multibacillary leprosy is started on dapsone. What is the primary mechanism of action of dapsone against Mycobacterium leprae?
opts: Inhibition of cell wall mycolic acid synthesis
Inhibition of protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit
questions.exp: Dapsone is a sulfone that competitively inhibits dihydropteroate synthetase, blocking para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) incorporation and folate synthesis in bacteria. Side effects include methemoglobinemia, haemolytic anaemia (G6PD deficiency), and dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome.

questions.q: A patient has a primary melanoma on the back with Breslow thickness 2.2 mm, no ulceration, mitotic rate <1/mm². No nodal or distant metastases are found. According to AJCC 8th edition, what is the correct T staging?
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition: T3 = 2.01–4.0 mm thickness; 'a' suffix = no ulceration. This melanoma at 2.2 mm without ulceration is T3a. T2 is 1.01–2.0 mm. The 'b' suffix denotes ulceration present.

questions.q: A 65-year-old fair-skinned farmer presents with a pearly translucent nodule with rolled edges and telangiectasias on the alar nose that bleeds on minor trauma. Histology shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral nuclear palisading and stromal retraction artifact. What is the most common subtype of basal cell carcinoma?
questions.exp: Nodular BCC is the most common subtype (60-80%), presenting as a pearly nodule with telangiectasia on the face. Histology shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. Morpheaform BCC is the most aggressive subtype and has the highest recurrence rate.

questions.q: A 35-year-old presents with well-demarcated silvery-scaled erythematous plaques on the elbows and knees. When scales are removed systematically, pinpoint bleeding points appear. What is this sign called and what is its histological basis?
opts: Auspitz sign — thinned suprapapillary plate with dilated capillaries in dermal papillae
Nikolsky sign — acantholysis at spinosum layer
questions.exp: Auspitz sign is the appearance of pinpoint bleeding after sequential removal of psoriatic scales (bulky scale → silvery scale → thin pellicle → bleeding points). It results from the thinned suprapapillary plate overlying elongated rete ridges with tortuous dilated capillaries in dermal papillae.

questions.q: A 70-year-old diabetic patient presents with vesicular eruption in the V1 trigeminal distribution with vesicles on the tip of the nose. Which finding most strongly indicates a need for IV antiviral therapy to prevent serious complications?
opts: Vesicles on tip of nose (Hutchinson's sign) suggesting nasociliary branch involvement
questions.exp: Hutchinson's sign (vesicles on the tip and side of the nose) indicates nasociliary branch involvement, predicting ocular complications including keratitis and uveitis. IV acyclovir is indicated for HZ ophthalmicus to prevent vision-threatening complications. Prompt ophthalmology referral is essential.

questions.q: A patient with borderline lepromatous leprosy (BL) develops multiple tender erythematous nodules on the extensor surfaces of limbs, high fever, arthralgia, and iridocyclitis. Nerve function assessment shows no new deficits. What type of lepra reaction is this and what is the immunological mechanism?
opts: Type 2 reaction (ENL) — immune complex mediated (Type III)
questions.exp: Type 2 (ENL) reaction occurs in BL and LL leprosy. It is an Arthus-type immune complex (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction with complement activation. Features: tender erythematous nodules, fever, iridocyclitis, orchitis, arthritis. Treatment: thalidomide (drug of choice for ENL, contraindicated in pregnancy) or steroids.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules over the knuckles, V-sign, and shawl sign. Which laboratory parameter is the most sensitive marker of muscle inflammation and is used to monitor treatment response?
questions.exp: CPK is the most sensitive and specific marker for active myositis in dermatomyositis and polymyositis. It is used to monitor treatment response. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with antisynthetase syndrome (ILD, mechanic's hands, Raynaud's). Anti-Mi-2 is specific for classic dermatomyositis with good prognosis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with multiple violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal pruritic papules on the flexor wrists with Wickham's striae and white lacy patches on the buccal mucosa. What is the characteristic histological finding?
opts: Acantholysis with intraepidermal blister above the basal layer
Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ with saw-tooth rete ridges and basal cell vacuolation
questions.exp: Lichen planus histology: hyperkeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, irregular saw-tooth rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ, basal cell vacuolation, and Civatte (colloid/hyaline) bodies representing necrotic keratinocytes. The mnemonic: H-WSBS-BVC (Hyperkeratosis, Wedge granulosis, Saw-tooth, Band, Vacuolation, Civatte bodies).

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with intense nocturnal pruritus, burrows in the interdigital spaces, and similar symptoms in multiple household members. What is the drug of choice for treatment of scabies in adults?
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the drug of choice for scabies. It is applied from neck to toe overnight and repeated after 1 week. It is safe in pregnancy and infants >2 months. Ivermectin is used for crusted (Norwegian) scabies and mass treatment campaigns. Lindane is avoided due to neurotoxicity. All household contacts must be treated simultaneously.

questions.q: A 17-year-old presents with comedones, papules, and pustules on the face. Which event is considered the primary/initiating step in the pathogenesis of acne vulgaris?
opts: Cutibacterium acnes (formerly P. acnes) colonization and biofilm formation
Follicular infundibular hyperkeratinization forming a microcomedo
Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1α) by keratinocytes
questions.exp: Follicular hyperkeratinization leading to microcomedo formation is the primary event in acne pathogenesis. The microcomedo is the precursor lesion, preceding all other changes. The sequence: (1) follicular hyperkeratinization, (2) sebum accumulation, (3) C. acnes proliferation, (4) inflammation. Isotretinoin addresses all four pathogenic factors.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with hypopigmented scaly macules on the chest and upper back that became more prominent after sun exposure. KOH preparation of skin scrapings shows a characteristic pattern. Which finding is expected?
opts: Short curved hyphae and clusters of yeast cells (spaghetti and meatballs)
questions.exp: Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor caused by Malassezia furfur shows characteristic 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern on KOH: short curved hyphae (spaghetti) and clusters of round spores (meatballs). Hypopigmentation is due to azelaic acid inhibiting tyrosinase. Treatment: ketoconazole shampoo, selenium sulfide, or single-dose oral itraconazole 400mg.

questions.q: A 32-year-old presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blisters with neutrophilic microabscesses at papillary tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae. Which associated systemic condition must be investigated?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is strongly associated with celiac disease in 80-90% of patients. Anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies are positive. Granular IgA at dermal papillae on DIF is pathognomonic. Treatment: dapsone for immediate relief, and a strict gluten-free diet for both skin and gut.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child develops widespread skin tenderness, fever, and large superficial blisters with peeling of skin in sheets. Nikolsky sign is positive on uninvolved skin. Blister fluid culture is sterile. At which level does the skin cleavage occur in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome?
questions.exp: In SSSS, S. aureus phage group II exfoliative toxins (ET-A, ET-B) cleave desmoglein 1 → separation within the stratum granulosum. Blister fluid is sterile as the toxin is haematogenously spread from a distant focus (conjunctivae, pharynx, umbilicus). In contrast, TEN shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis with cleavage at the DEJ.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with soft, cauliflower-like papillomatous lesions on the glans penis. HPV typing shows HPV-6 and HPV-11. Which statement about management is correct?
opts: HPV 6 and 11 are high-risk types requiring immediate wide local excision
HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types; podophyllin 25% is a topical treatment option (avoid in pregnancy)
Systemic antiviral therapy with acyclovir is curative
Immediate circumcision is the first-line treatment
questions.exp: HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types causing condyloma acuminata with rare malignant transformation. Treatment options: podophyllin 25% (avoid in pregnancy), imiquimod 5% cream, TCA, cryotherapy, or surgical excision. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic types. Giant condyloma of Buschke-Löwenstein is associated with HPV 6/11 but is locally destructive.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with purulent urethral discharge for 3 days. Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes. What is the currently recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea?
opts: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 1g oral
Penicillin G 4.8 MU IM with probenecid
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Current WHO/CDC guidelines recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose (1g if weight >150 kg) plus azithromycin 1g for uncomplicated gonorrhoea, due to widespread fluoroquinolone resistance. Azithromycin also covers presumptive Chlamydia co-infection. Penicillin and quinolone resistance are widespread globally.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with skin tightening over fingers, Raynaud's phenomenon, telangiectasias, and calcinosis. She has limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome). Which antibody is most characteristic of this subtype?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is characteristic of limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome) and predicts risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension but not ILD. Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) is seen in diffuse cutaneous SSc with ILD. Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with diffuse SSc and scleroderma renal crisis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with superficial erosions and crusted plaques on the face, scalp, and trunk with no oral mucosal involvement. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG in the upper epidermis. What is the autoantigen, and why is the oral mucosa spared?
opts: Desmoglein 3; oral mucosa is spared because DSG3 is expressed only in the skin
Desmoglein 1; oral mucosa is spared because DSG3 (unaffected) compensates in mucosae
BP180; no blister occurs in mucosae as hemidesmosomes are absent there
Plakophilin 1; its low expression in mucosae provides protection
questions.exp: Pemphigus foliaceus targets desmoglein 1 only. Oral mucosa is spared because desmoglein 3 (which is highly expressed in the mucosa) compensates for the loss of desmoglein 1 function there, maintaining cell adhesion. This is the desmoglein compensation theory. PF causes superficial (subcorneal/granular layer) blistering.

questions.q: A patient with severe chronic plaque psoriasis is being considered for methotrexate therapy. Which monitoring strategy is currently recommended to detect methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity?
opts: LFTs every 3 months; no biopsy needed unless LFTs persistently abnormal
Serum PIIINP (procollagen III aminoterminal peptide) every 3 months OR liver biopsy after every 1.5g cumulative dose
Serum creatinine and CBC only; hepatotoxicity risk is negligible at standard doses
Annual chest X-ray to detect pulmonary fibrosis as a surrogate for hepatic fibrosis
questions.exp: Traditional guidelines recommend liver biopsy after every 1.5–2g cumulative MTX dose. Newer guidelines accept PIIINP (marker of hepatic fibrosis) every 2-3 months as a non-invasive alternative; persistently elevated levels warrant biopsy or FibroScan. Folic acid supplementation reduces haematological/mucosal toxicity but not hepatotoxicity.

questions.q: A 28-year-old with segmental vitiligo on the face involving 5% BSA requests phototherapy. Which phototherapy modality is considered the gold standard for vitiligo repigmentation?
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB (311-313 nm) is the gold standard phototherapy for vitiligo. It stimulates melanocyte migration from perilesional skin and hair follicle reservoirs. Advantages over PUVA: no psoralen required, safe in children and pregnancy, no GI side effects. Excimer laser (308 nm) is preferred for focal/recalcitrant lesions due to higher fluence.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male with a long history of psoriasis develops generalised erythema and scaling covering >90% BSA, with fever, tachycardia, pedal oedema, and hypoalbuminaemia. What is the most common underlying cause of erythroderma in adults?
questions.exp: Pre-existing dermatosis (psoriasis ~25%, atopic dermatitis ~25%) is the most common cause of erythroderma, accounting for ~50% of cases. Drug reactions account for ~20%, and lymphoma/leukaemia (Sézary syndrome) for ~10%. Idiopathic erythroderma accounts for ~20%. Complications: protein/electrolyte loss, thermoregulatory failure, high-output cardiac failure.

questions.q: A 35-year-old cardiologist on long-term amiodarone therapy develops blue-grey discolouration on sun-exposed areas of the face and dorsal hands. Which type of photosensitivity reaction does amiodarone typically cause?
questions.exp: Amiodarone causes a phototoxic reaction (dose-dependent, not immune-mediated, occurs in all individuals at sufficient doses) leading to blue-grey pigmentation from iodine deposition. Phototoxic drugs: amiodarone, psoralens, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, NSAIDs (naproxen), thiazides. Photoallergic reactions (Type IV, eczematous) are caused by sulfonamides, PABA sunscreens, benzophenones.
